rv.q: Rarely have I spent so entertaining a night at the theater—or witnessed so touching a tribute to a departed parent.
Precious, to anyone who sees 'Stories by Heart,' is the loving way son has chosen to pay tribute to father.
It’s gratifying to watch this actor make his formidable application to this exclusive theatrical club.

"Lithgow first takes on the role of a gossipy Midwestern barber in Lardner’s 'Haircut'...Lithgow’s uncharacteristically subdued delivery, which befits Lardner’s dismal tone, further taxes our powers of concentration. What results is a scrupulous rendition that nonetheless seems to lack an extra theatrical dimension.
It is a pleasant way to stay put on a winter's night.
And when he dives into the words and worlds of Lardner and Wodehouse, Stories by Heart is pure entertainment of the most ancient and appealing kind.
And then give him one for spiritual effects, because “Stories by Heart” is delightful: illuminating the stories, uplifting us.
They all are exceedingly good company.

He makes a brilliant buffoon of the oblivious barber, allowing himself no more than a delighted and slightly demented cackle to let us in on the joke of this “light comedy of small town American life that slowly turns into a gruesome tale of misogyny, adultery, and murder.”

Overall, Lithgow’s formidable acting prowess ensures that “Stories By Heart” is a largely heartwarming evening that charms within its modest conventions, even though it occasionally falls short of compelling.
But despite the performer’s estimable talents, John Lithgow: Stories by Heart smacks mainly of self-indulgence.
So it is both a pleasure and a disappointment to find him
But dramatically, and as a work of cohesive storytelling, the outwardly sentimental show has little in the way of heft.
The result is a tour-de-force that, among other things, makes you wish the actor was available for private reading of bedtime stories.
Gratifyingly, his ‘Stories By Heart’ is written and staged with deceptive simplicity, and entirely avoids any air of the didactic

It was also while John was growing up that Arthur Lithgow gathered his children and read stories to them from a large book: Tellers of Tales, which contains 100 Classic Short Stories (as selected by W. Somerset Maugham), including the two that serve as the centerpiece of this particular play.

His performance is enthralling, and he elicits an appropriately shifting reaction from the audience, as the mood of the story becomes increasingly dark and disturbing, and Kendall gets his ultimate comeuppance – much to the clueless dismay of the barber.
This one-man show has artistry as well as Heart.
It is a pleasure to witness Lithgow demonstrate his proficiency as an actor while honoring both his father and the power of the spoken word.

These amount to something of a memoir of his father, and it is no denigration of the short stories to say that Lithgow’s well-told personal anecdotes are what provide much of the heart in Stories by Heart.
This is ultimately a basic piece of theater that never really digs below its cozy, slightly drab surface.

"Lithgow is charming and a physically as well as vocally masterful storyteller...But whether two recreated remembrances of stories his father told to him at his siblings when they were young, is really a theatrical outing worth the high price of admission depends on whether you share Lithgow's enthusiasm for this type of storytelling...
Mr. Lithgow is always colorful, but here he is coloring well within the lines.
But despite the performer's estimable talents, John Lithgow: Stories by Heart smacks mainly of self-indulgence.
"Stories By Heart" doesn't quite work that same magic.
Despite Lithgow's acting prowess and the nostalgic appeal that Stories by Heart promises, director Daniel Sullivan hasn't whipped things up enough to make the show into engaging theater.
While the tidbits Lithgow shares about his family and his presentation of "Uncle Fred Flits By" are decidedly entertaining, these are not enough to justify the evening.
But even the best literature has limited appeal to a mainstream theatre audience.
There is great skill to what Lithgow is attempting, but the exercise is also oddly airless and feels a little pointless.
Each story is delivered with polish, precision and complete characterization — and yet, each can be hard to follow and turn into a bore.

Like that moment of show-and-tell, the not-inconsiderable pleasures of “Stories by Heart” are entirely too slight for a Broadway house, like a championship Scrabble game held in Madison Square Garden.

He has the uncanny ability to remain the consummate professional actor, working out all the nuances of great acting and storytelling and narration, while at the exact same time inviting us in to the most vulnerable and intimate moments of his life.

Congenial, involving, and totally entertaining, the Roundabout Theatre Company’s “Stories by Heart” shows the lasting emotional resonance a really good story can have, especially when it means something very special to the person doing the telling.
Lithgow’s comic timing and juggling of spot-on voices is impeccable.
Stories by Heart is thoroughly sincere and sentimental, which I find very refreshing.
This is a character actor at the top of his form, his personal likeableness enhancing the appeal his long career has established for Broadway audiences.
Even in a large Broadway house, it’s an extremely intimate evening with the brilliant Lithgow.
Few performers possess the charisma and, frankly, the chops to straddle a stage alone and draw you in so fully – but Lithgow might be that great exception.
Stories by Heart, a very personal, mostly entertaining memoir, from one of our finest actors.
His performance in his “Stories By Heart” is no exception to those expectations.
I enjoyed the family reminiscences he recounted before each story more than the stories themselves.
Stories by Heart is sweet, engaging, sentimental, and charming, with some laughs and tender smiles mixed in to the batch, but also a bit too easy and dull on the ears, mind, and heart.
His movements are so precise and his concentration so unflinching that we can’t help but believe there is a towel, a leather strap, a razor, and a flesh and blood customer.

cn.t: Critics praise Lithgow's masterful storytelling and warm charisma, but many find the material slight and better suited to a more intimate venue than Broadway. His performance of two vintage short stories earns admiration, though personal anecdotes resonate more.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
